content.eyebrow: Home Addition Contractors in Western Washington
content.headline: Which type of addition fits your home?
content.body: The best addition type depends on the space you need, the existing structure, the property, access, utilities, and local requirements.

steps.title: Bump-out addition
steps.copy: A bump-out extends part of the existing footprint to create more usable room. It may suit a kitchen, dining area, bedroom, or other space when a smaller expansion can solve the problem.

steps.title: Second-story addition
steps.copy: Building upward can add living area without extending the footprint, but the existing structure, access, utilities, and design all need careful review.

steps.title: Attached ADU
steps.copy: An attached accessory dwelling unit adds a separate living arrangement within or alongside the existing home. Layout, privacy, access, utilities, and local requirements all shape the conversation.

steps.title: Detached DADU
steps.copy: A detached accessory dwelling unit creates a separate structure on the same property. Site placement, setbacks, utilities, access, and local requirements must be reviewed before a plan is treated as feasible.

content.headline: What an addition contractor manages
content.body: A successful addition has to connect to the home you already have. The planning conversation should account for design-build coordination, permit questions, structural work, the connection between new and existing spaces, material decisions, and the handoff between each stage. Tubro's assigned project manager gives homeowners a clear point of contact as the scope develops and construction moves forward. Tubro Construction is veteran-owned and was founded in 2010 by Rich Tietjen, a U.S. Army veteran. The team brings that communication-first mindset to the planning conversation and the work that follows. Have questions about a home addition, ADU, or DADU? Book Your Free Estimate or call 253-216-2633 to start the conversation.

content.eyebrow: Home Addition Contractors in Western Washington
content.headline: Start with the lot, not just the wish list
content.body: A home addition has to fit both the household and the property. In King County or Pierce County, the early feasibility conversation may include zoning, setbacks, utilities, septic or sewer conditions, site access, grading, and the way the addition will connect to the existing structure. Requirements vary by property and jurisdiction. Tubro can help identify the questions to review, but no contractor should promise approval before the applicable requirements are confirmed.

steps.title: Zoning, setbacks, and site access
steps.copy: The available building area, required setbacks, driveway or work access, and the location of existing structures can affect which addition concepts are practical.

steps.title: Utilities and existing conditions
steps.copy: Electrical, plumbing, heating, sewer or septic, foundation, and structural conditions may shape the design and the work needed to connect new space to the existing home.

content.eyebrow: Home Addition Contractors in Western Washington
content.headline: What shapes the cost of a home addition
content.body: There is no useful one-size-fits-all price for an addition. Scope, size, structure, foundation work, utility changes, site access, design requirements, permits, materials, and finish selections all affect the project. A free estimate is the right place to discuss the home, the goal, and the level of work involved. Upfront pricing helps make the scope visible; it is not a promise of a fixed project price before those details are known.

content.eyebrow: Home Addition Contractors in Western Washington
content.headline: Questions homeowners ask about additions
content.body: Clear answers help homeowners decide which questions to bring to an estimate conversation.
bullets: Can Tubro Construction help with a home addition in my area? Tubro Construction serves homeowners in King County and Pierce County in Western Washington. Start with the property location, the space you want to add, and what the new space needs to do.

Is an attached ADU different from a detached DADU? Yes. An attached ADU is connected to or part of the existing home, while a detached DADU is a separate structure on the same property. The layout, access, utilities, site conditions, and local requirements can differ.

Will my home addition need permits? Many structural additions require permits, but the exact requirements depend on the project and jurisdiction. Permit questions should be confirmed for the specific property before construction plans are treated as approved.

Can you tell me whether my lot can support an addition? Tubro can help start a feasibility conversation around the home, lot, access, utilities, and intended scope. Final feasibility and approval depend on the applicable property and jurisdiction requirements.

How much does a home addition cost? The cost depends on the size, design, structural connection, foundation, utilities, site conditions, materials, finish choices, and permit or design requirements. Request a free estimate to discuss the actual home and scope instead of relying on a generic figure.
